name: Diospyros

project_scope.selection_mode: Both existing manifest-installed Diospyros species; Texas persimmon field anchor and American persimmon eastern-range look-alike
project_scope.native_metrics_note: D. texana PASS (Hays, Travis, Mason; Williamson excluded as out-of-target); D. virginiana UNRESOLVED for project counties (only Travis verified) and learner-approved comparison.
project_scope.source_policy: Leave regional native-range decisions separate from species admission; do not count Williamson as one of the 24 target-zone counties.

shared_traits: Ebenaceae woody trees/shrubs with ALTERNATE SIMPLE leaves and usually entire margins; NOT compound-leaf legumes.
Flowers small, usually bell- or urn-shaped with fused petals (sympetalous); ovary superior.
Persimmon fruit is a fleshy BERRY rather than a dry capsule or drupe, often with a conspicuous persistent green calyx beneath it.
Flowers have male (staminate) and female (pistillate) function; reproductive arrangement should not be inferred from one flower without inspecting its organs.
Bark is valuable on mature trees but can be less diagnostic on saplings; pair bark with leaf size/underside and calyx-fruit evidence.
priority: FIRST: smooth pale mottled or peeling mature bark versus deeply fissured dark square-blocky bark.

SECOND: Texas persimmon typically has SHORT obovate leaves ~1.5–3.5 cm with rolled-under margins and pale fuzzy undersides; American persimmon leaves often longer, more pointed, and mostly much larger.
THIRD: Texas persimmon fruits black/purple-black at maturity; American persimmon fruits yellowish-orange to reddish-orange.
FOURTH: both retain broad persistent sepals at the fruit base; inspect the persistent CALYX.
FIFTH: flowering position and leaf underside hairs add supporting confidence when fruit is missing.
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify an unripe green persimmon by color; both species start green. Mature bark and leaf structure are stronger when fruits absent. Important source disagreement: most sources call Texas persimmon dioecious; UT Williamson flora calls it monoecious. Do not use plant sex alone as the key.

quick_key.if: smooth light gray exfoliating trunk + small (usually 1.5–3.5 cm) obovate leaves with fuzzy undersides and rolled margins
dark gray, deeply checked blocky mature trunk + leaves generally about 3.5–8 cm, often pointed
a ripe black/purple-black fuzzy berry with large persistent calyx, on small-leaved shrub/tree
a ripe yellow-orange/reddish fruit with persistent broad green calyx, on larger-leaved tree
smooth ornamental peeling bark but OPPOSITE leaves and woody dry capsules rather than persimmon berries
quick_key.then: Lagerstroemia indica — crape myrtle, NOT Diospyros

look_here_first: Read the mature bark first: Texas persimmon smooth pale mottled trunks; American persimmon thick dark square-blocked bark. Confirm with SMALL rounded rolled-edge leaves versus larger mostly pointed leaves. Black versus orange ripe fruit locks the ID.

visual_comparison.title: Texas persimmon vs American persimmon — five real-photo ID checks
visual_comparison.subtitle: See the contrast in actual bark and fruit photographs; arrows point to obvious visible parts, never imagined microscopic structures.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: TEXAS: smooth pale trunks + tiny rolled leaves + black fruit. AMERICAN: dark blocky bark + larger leaves + orange fruit.
